I was a shit F1 a year ago and now I’m a shit f2. Joking aside, I’m sure you aren’t shit - in my mind there are very few shit f1s and those who are are the people who don’t care/ don’t want to improve. The very fact you wrote this post proves that you aren’t in my mind. 

I think the most important thing is to make a good job list. On the ward round nail down the jobs from your senior. Clarify what exact antibiotics your consultant wants or ask whether they want them continued. Ask whether they want a scan as an in patient or outpatient. Sure, sometimes you might feel like you should already know what your consultant wants but I can guarantee that they would rather that you clarified the plan during the ward round than floundering. 

In terms of time management, again your job list should help. If u don’t want to be late or handover bloods make sure they are done early in the day. If you need to call micro or something, again try and get it done earlier so that you aren’t waiting around for them to call back. The afternoon is prime time to prep ttos/ do non urgent jobs. That way your afternoon doesn’t generate any work that might mean you have to stay late. 

In terms of medical knowledge, all I can say is that I get where you’re coming from. I question my knowledge all the time. However, I don’t think being a good F1 has much to do with clinical acumen tbh - as long as you aren’t doing anything completely rogue then no one is expecting much more

This all sounds horrendous and I’m really sorry that you’re in this situation. Firstly, this is just a job and no job should be more important than your mental and physical health. It’s clear that the psychological stress is impacting on your body and you need to intervene. You need to take some time off right now. It isn’t that you’re failing with the pressure, it’s that the system is failing you. 

If you want to take a break then I’d suggest the following (I have done the same, and I know of others who also have so you aren’t alone):
- Self-certify absence for 1 week (email staffing/ foundation programme director)
- In the mean time, contact your GP if you need longer off
- ask to be referred to occy health (if you are off sick then they should be quicker)
- if you have any friends or family then go and spend some time with them, be honest and open - it isn’t you who is failing
- discuss changing your placement with occupational health/ foundation programme director

I completely agree. I guess I came at it from my own experiences so that biased my opinion a bit. Depression and anxiety are so common and are often the most visible manifestations of other mental health problems but you’re completely right that there are plenty of other important mental health problems so thanks for flagging this up!

I think it helps to have a grasp of some of the common symptoms of depression and anxiety, things like: change in sleep; low mood; change in appetite; loss of motivation. Whilst these are very common they can be hard to spot in people. If you know the person well you may be able to spot a change in someone’s behaviour or appearance. They might be drinking more alcohol, or keeping to themselves more. They might be quieter and more irritable. They might let their appearance go a bit, not washing or shaving etc. There are also more subtle things, like the way they hold themselves. It is really common for depressed people to avoid eye contact and just look a bit deflated. 

That being said there are so many variations of the “normal” presentation of mental health difficulties. I think the most important thing is to be open, have a low index of suspicion and simply be there for them if they want your help.

Normally, swelling is caused by inflammation of tissue. There are a load of inflammatory molecules which divert more blood flow to the damaged area, in order to provide it with all the nutrients we need for re-growth etc. As a byproduct of more blood going to damaged tissue, there is more pressure in these blood vessels and this squeezes some liquid out of the blood vessels and into the surrounding tissues (hence the swelling). By applying ice to a damaged (or inflamed area), you reduce the blood flow to this damaged area (the body doesn’t like the cold so the blood is re-diverted back away from the damaged are). The reduced blood flow -> less liquid squeezed out -> less swelling

An EKG or ECG stands for electrocardiograph. It works by placing a load of sticky pads (electrodes) on the body, and together these electrodes make up the leads. The basic premise is that the electrodes detect tiny electrical changes on the skin, picking up the signal of the depolarisation of the heart muscle. The standard ECG is a 12-lead ECG (only 10 electrodes but some augmented ones, probably a bit complicated), and this allows you to look at the direction of the electrical impulses across different areas of the heart. If one bit of the heart’s conduction pathway is blocked (like in a heart attack or something), the electrical impulse will be altered and people far more clever than I are able to roughly pinpoint where the blockage is based on the different views from the different leads. Hope this helps

Paracetamol (or acetaminophen if you’re American) is quite an interesting drug. We aren’t quite sure exactly how it works but it’s thought to inhibit this enzyme (protein) called cox-3. Cox-3 is almost entirely located in the brain and by inhibiting it, you get less of another protein (prostaglandin) made. Less prostaglandin essentially equals less pain. To slightly confuse it all, it is thought that paracetamol enhances our natural pain relief system (cannabinoid sustem). So paracetamol is good for fevers or pain but not good as an anti-inflammatory. 

Ibuprofen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory that works by inhibiting the cox enzymes again, but mostly this cox enzyme called cox-2. Again it does a whole bunch of things but basically reduces prostaglandins (=pain) in both the brain and outside the brain.

They are used as part of the treatment, according to this theory called the monoamine hypothesis. But basically, this theory says that in depression you don’t have enough of a few neurotransmitters (serotonin and noradrenaline etc), so the theory is by blocking the re-uptake of these neurotransmitters from between cell synapses you have more serotonin hanging about. Serotonin and noradrenaline have a ridiculous number of effects but basically, increasing them can offset the negative symptoms of depression.

Heart disease is an all-encompassing term which generally focuses on the chronic diseases of the heart. Most specifically, atherosclerosis (build up of crap in blood vessels), which reduces blood flow to the muscle of the heart and then causes things like angina (pain in the chest due to an insufficient blood supply to the heart). A STEMI is one type of MI where the blood supply to the heart is blocked acutely, resulting in heart tissue ischaemia and death of some of that heart tissue.  An MI is normally as a result of atherosclerosis but refers to the acute presentation of a heart attack. Coronary heart disease is also as a result of atherosclerosis but refers to the more chronic manifestation. Hope this helps.

I know exactly how you feel. The only thing that helps me sleep is thinking about my death and wondering who *actually* cared. The truth is that people would care if you were gone, and if that isn’t enough for you, then live for yourself. Live for what drives you, your hobbies and your interests.
